2.1 Device configuration (option bytes, not supposed to be modified ever)
• Use RDP level 2 or Closed (Locked) product state. This closes the device from any external access.
2.2 Remove debug capability for the device.
• Use product life cycle or RDP level 2 for disabling the debug. Some devices allow usage of debug authentication (DA).
2.3 Protect a device against a loss of external clock source (crystal).
2.5 Protect a device from code injection.

• Use the RDP or product life cycle. • Isolate communication port protocol with the MPU, firewall, or HDP. • Limit communication port protocol access range. • Use write protection on empty memory areas (flash memory and SRAM).
3. Code protection against internal threats: TrustZone, PCROP, MPU, firewall, and HDP
3. Code protection against internal threats: TrustZone, PCROP, MPU, firewall, and HDP
• Use RDP level 2 against external access. • Use PCROP on most sensitive parts of the code against internal read access. • Use OTFDEC to secure code stored in the external memory.
3.2 Protect secret data from other processes.
• Use firewall to protect both code and data. • Use MPU to protect secret data area from being read. • Use HDP in case data must only be used at reset. • Use secure domain of TrustZone, if available.
3.3 Protect code and data when not fully verified or trusted libraries are used.

• Use PCROP to protect user most sensitive code. • Use firewall to protect user sensitive application (code, data, and execution). • Use MPU and de-privilege the untrusted library. • Use IWDG to avoid any deadlock. • Use secure domain of TrustZone, if available.
4. Device security check and maintenance: integrity checks, SB, SFU
4. Device security check and maintenance: integrity checks, SB, SFU
• Hash firmware code at reset and compare to expected value. • Enable ECC on the flash memory and parity check on the SRAM.
4.2 Security checks or embedded firmware authentication
4.3 Securely update the firmware in the field.
• Implement a SFU application with cryptography. • Apply relevant secure memory protection around the SFU secret data (refer to previous sections).
• Use or implement secure communication stacks relying on cryptography for confidentiality and authentication (such as TLS for Ethernet).
5.2 Use the ST AES/SHA cryptographic functions with STM32 devices.
• Use only official software implementation by ST with STM32 X-CUBE-CRYPTOLIB.
• Use device with cryptographic hardware peripheral together with official STM32 X-CUBE-CRYPTOLIB. • Use MCE or OTFDEC to access AES-ciphered code in the external memory without latency penalty.
• Use RNG embedded in the STM32 devices.
• Embed a shared encryption key in the device, and exchange encrypted message.
• Embed a device private key and its certificate in the device, and exchange encrypted message.
• Embed a shared encryption key in the device, and exchange encrypted message. • Embed server public key in the device, and exchange encrypted message.
• Use OBK where available. • Use SAES and CCB to prevent exposing key. • After usage, clean-up exposed key or intermediate data.

_notes: 4. Device security check and maintenance: integrity checks, SB, SFU
